newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Australia wants bans on nuclear material, landmines.
newsitem.headline: Australia wants bans on nuclear material, landmines.

text.p: Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer called on Monday for an international convention barring any further manufacture of weapons grade nuclear material and another banning landmines.

"Having at last, after 33 years, met the challenge of CTBT (Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty), the international community must now push on with further practical and realistic measures on nuclear arms control and disarmament," he said in a speech to the General Assembly.

Australia played a leading role earlier this month in getting the Assembly to adopt the CTBT, banning all nuclear test explosions. Representatives of more than 100 countries subscribed since it was opened for signature September 24. But it will not enter into force until all 44 nations with nuclear reactors have signed and ratified the treaty.

Downer said one of the next steps towards nuclear arms control and disarmament was the "negotiation of a convention under which it would be agreed that there will be no further manufacturing of weapons-grade fissile material. This convention should be sought now," he said.
Any discussion of arms control which failed to address the question of landmines would be "sadly incomplete," he added.
"These hideous and diabolically inexpensive weapons must be banned," he said, pledging Australia's support for efforts at the current Assembly to negotiate such an international convention.
He also called for faster action to clear more than 100 million mines scattered throughout many countries.

Australia proposed the establishment of a technological working group among interested and capable countries to design the equipment required for de-mining on a far larger and quicker scale than hitherto.
If the current rate of de-mining in Cambodia were maintained, he said, it would not be free of mines for another 130 years.

On the issue of enlarging the Security Council, which currently has five permanent members -- the United States, Russia, Britain, China and France -- and 10 non-permanent members which each serve two-year terms, he said:

"Australia has made clear that it supports the claims of Japan and Germany to permanent membership. This is the very least the United Nations can do to acknowledge their major-power status and the financial contribution they are making to the organisation," Downer said.

"Australia also advocates permanent seats on the council for under-represented regions," he said, but it was flexible on whether each of those seats should be filled by a single member or rotate among leading member states agreed on by regional groupings.
